store.0: I am a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed with higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basic quantum computing. It's exciting to see how much I've grown as a student.
store.1: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving, like optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The kind of problems that fascinate me are those that require dynamic programming approaches or approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great; she has a knack for explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll put up a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing.
store.2: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is definitely an adventure. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas of what the final product should look like. But that's also the beauty of it, right? In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle everything from concurrency issues to node failures gracefully. It's nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.3: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. My professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even some user experience design. It's incredibly fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about finding the perfect balance for the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.
store.4: I also have an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be intimidating, but I'm actually enjoying it now. The professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than just math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not building actual quantum computers, but we're modeling algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff that's changing how I approach problems.
store.5: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is basically the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It sounds fancy, but essentially, we're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts by analyzing a firehose of tweets or posts for words that suggest a disaster or crisis. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to stay organized. One person on our team is the designated Scrum Master, so we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.6: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it applies to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.7: I'm juggling a typical college schedule. Mondays and Wednesdays are packed. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload.
store.8: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. Capstone alone can consume around ten hours a week, more if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly. The Distributed Systems project is another time-sucking endeavor. My group meets at least twice a week, and we rely on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a logistical nightmare. However, despite the stress, it's also exhilarating. This is one of my last chances to fully immerse myself in an academic project without the pressures of a real-world job environment. It's a great opportunity to learn and grow.
store.9: I'm having a blast overall. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, especially if something's due the next day and I'm stuck debugging. However, it's no longer as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a great feeling.
store.10: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and my hobbies are what keep me sane amidst the chaos of classes and projects. It's interesting how coding can be both intense and enjoyable at the same time. I find that my outside interests help me approach programming with a fresh perspective. Taking breaks is essential, as it prevents me from being stuck behind my laptop 24/7. I believe it's crucial to have a balance between work and play.
store.11: Sailing is probably the first thing that comes to mind when people ask about my hobbies. It's unique among my friends, and I'm grateful to have grown up near a beautiful marina. My dad used to take me out on these tiny sailboats when I was younger, and the moment I felt the rush of wind against the sails, I was hooked. Now in college, I try to keep up with sailing whenever I go back home for breaks. There's a local sailing club that rents out boats at a student-friendly rate, so I'll sign up for a day, invite a friend if they want to join, and spend hours on the water. I love the sense of freedom it gives me. Everything else – looming deadlines, bug fixes in code, group project drama – fades into the background. Out there, the water's choppy, the wind's unpredictable, and you've got to stay focused. It's like a puzzle on a grand scale, which might be why it appeals to my problem-solving side.
store.12: I used to be the scrawny kid in high school who spent most of his time hunched over a computer. However, once I got to college, I realized I needed something to offset the hours spent sitting in front of a screen. I started with a basic lifting routine in my freshman year. A friend from my dorm taught me the fundamentals, such as proper form for squats and deadlifts, how to program workouts, and other essential skills. Now, I try to hit the gym around four times a week. It's not about becoming a bodybuilder; I just enjoy seeing incremental improvements. If I can lift a bit more weight this month than last, or if I have more energy in my daily life, I consider that a win. Additionally, it's a great stress-reliever after marathon coding sessions. The mental clarity I get after a good workout is incredible. It makes me more productive and helps me sleep better, especially on nights when I'm up late finishing an assignment.
store.13: Gaming is another hobby that's almost an extension of my interest in technology. I'm a fan of both PC and console games, but I spend more time on PC since it's my best friend as a CS major. Lately, I've been really into co-op survival games where you gather resources, build shelters, fend off creatures, and so on. I enjoy problem-solving in a more relaxed environment compared to debugging a large codebase. Occasionally, I also jump into fast-paced shooters, especially if some friends from class are online and want to team up. It's both social and mentally challenging for me. While some people view gaming as a waste of time, I believe it can be strategic and collaborative. It's also a great way to stay connected. I've dabbled in game development using Unity or Unreal Engine for fun. I'd like to explore this further if time allows, as bridging the gap between playing games and creating them is fascinating.
store.14: Reading has been a part of me since I was a kid. My mom, who's a huge literature buff, used to hand me fantasy and sci-fi novels. I'd get lost in other worlds for hours on end. Even with a cramped schedule now, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends when I have a spare hour. Lately, I've been obsessed with sci-fi that deals with artificial intelligence. It's partly driven by my academic interests, to be honest. I enjoy imagining future technology and how it might blur the boundaries between humans and machines. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. Books like that help me consider the ethical and social implications of what I'm studying. In a way, reading isn't just relaxation; it's also helping me explore more philosophical questions about the work I'll be doing after graduation.
store.15: I might think that juggling all these hobbies would be chaotic, but I've found that scheduling them helps me maintain a healthy balance. I take a look at my week every Sunday and plan accordingly. If the weather is nice, I'll head to the gym in the afternoon or drive out to the local lake to rent a dinghy for a few hours. If not, I'll plan an indoor day with friends, either playing co-op games or working out in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to fit in – I do 30 minutes before bedtime, which is a great way to unwind after a long day.
store.16: I've found that combining hobbies can be a great way to enhance the experience. For example, I once spent the morning sailing at the lake, followed by lunch, and then spent the evening playing video games with friends. It was fascinating to notice how the experience on the water was similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op. In both cases, everyone has a role – whether it's managing the sails or leading the in-game strategy. I love how each hobby, in its own way, demands teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. It's amazing how these different activities can complement each other and bring out different aspects of my personality.
store.17: It can be stressful, no doubt. A significant portion of my day is consumed by lectures, labs, homework, research group meetings, and my part-time gig as a tutor for intro-level CS courses. However, if you're passionate about your hobbies, you'll always find a way to make time for them, even if it's just in small increments. For example, I might not be able to read for hours on end, but I can read one chapter. I might not be able to sail every weekend, but once a month works. And gaming? If I have 30 minutes to spare, that's enough to squeeze in a quick match. It's all about finding that balance and making the most of the time you have.
store.18: The best part about my hobbies is that they give me something to talk about outside of coding. I'm not saying I don't enjoy discussing data structures and algorithms – I do! However, it's great to have other interests that showcase a different side of me. My hobby menu ranges from the calming experience of reading to the thrill of sailing, from the discipline of weightlifting to the adrenaline rush of co-op games. It makes life interesting, you know? I'm glad I have these diverse hobbies to explore and share with others.
store.19: Archie is three years old now, and we got him when I was in my second year of college. My parents surprised both me and my sister with him during one of our winter breaks. We'd always talked about wanting a dog, especially a big, friendly breed that likes to run around and play catch. When I walked through the front door and saw Archie - tiny and fluffy, wagging that little tail like it was Christmas every day - my heart melted. Even though I was only back home for about three weeks during that break, I spent every moment I could getting to know him, taking him for short walks(he was too small for long ones at first), and teaching him random commands. I vividly remember how he'd tumble over himself trying to figure out 'sit' and 'stay'. It's wild how big he's gotten now - he's definitely not that little furball anymore!
store.20: Since I live on campus and only visit home on some weekends or during breaks, my parents do most of the day-to-day care for Archie. However, I video call them almost daily—kind of a running habit ever since my freshman year—and Archie always seems to recognize my voice. My mom will tilt the phone so he can see me, and he'll go nuts, wagging his tail and whining like he's about to jump through the screen. It's equal parts hilarious and heartwarming. In a weird way, those moments help me de-stress from back-to-back coding assignments or the infinite debugging sessions I find myself in. Someone once told me that dogs don't really perceive images on screens the way humans do, but Archie 100% knows something's up. Maybe it's just my voice that triggers him, but it's nice to believe he's looking right at me.
store.21: Family-wise, I'm pretty lucky. My dad is a software engineer, so he's part of the reason I got into computer science in the first place. We used to do these small coding exercises together when I was in high school. He'd challenge me to figure out a puzzle or a problem, and it sparked that early fascination with logic and technology that eventually led me to major in CS. My mom, on the other hand, works as a nurse. She's the most caring person I know, and she's always the emotional backbone of our family. Even if it's late at night, she'll pick up my calls when I need a pep talk or if I'm worried about an upcoming exam. Between my parents, I found this healthy balance: I got the analytical edge from my dad and the empathetic side from my mom. My sister, well, she's just a ball of energy - constantly on social media, playing new games, or looking for the next big trend. She's so plugged into technology that sometimes she jokes she's going to overshadow me in the tech scene. She might be right.
store.22: Anyway, every time I go home, Archie greets me like I've been gone for centuries. He bounds around, does that little circle dance, and basically tries to tackle me to the ground in excitement. One of our family traditions is going on a Saturday morning hike whenever I'm in town. We pack some snacks, load Archie into our SUV, and drive out to this trail about twenty minutes away. The path isn't super long, but it has a great view at the summit of a small bluff that overlooks a lake. Archie loves it - he's got endless energy. By the time we're at the top, he's chasing squirrels and sniffing every tree. Watching him run around like that reminds me to appreciate the small things. I can get so wrapped up in code and classes that I forget to just breathe and enjoy nature.
store.23: My extended family includes my grandparents, who live a state away. They mean so much to me. My grandma still teases me about the time I broke her antique vase when I was in middle school by throwing a mini football around her living room. I try to tune out that story, even though it's retold almost every Thanksgiving. Growing up, my family always valued spending time with relatives, so holiday gatherings are a big deal. Thanksgiving is practically a potluck extravaganza, with all kinds of dishes that make you want to hibernate until Christmas. Archie, of course, tries to snag anything that drops on the floor. We learned the hard way he has a sensitive stomach—one year he got into some leftover turkey bones, and we had to make a late-night veterinary visit. Ever since then, we're super careful about what 'people food' he can get his paws on.
